global.headline: IRAN HITS BAHRAIN A SECOND TIME, THE GULF TURNS ON TEHRAN, AND WASHINGTON WAITS
summary: The Bahrain Defence Force said on Sunday it had intercepted and destroyed several Iranian drones, two days after a near-identical interception. The Revolutionary Guards claimed six drones against American radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base; US ambassador Stephanie Hallett called that false, said all were shot down and reported no injuries or damage. Bahrain's foreign ministry held Tehran fully responsible. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt condemned the attack, and GCC secretary-general Jasem Al Budaiwi called it a “blatant challenge” to the peace effort. The GCC opened an advanced headquarters in Kuwait last week for its unified military command.

The GCC has also begun demanding Iran compensate its neighbours for attacks on their territory — what Iran demands of Washington. Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei asked how states that made their airspace and waters available to those who attacked Iran could seek compensation from it, and warned the Gulf “must be careful not to reopen old wounds” — their support for Saddam Hussein in the 1980s. Asked whether Tehran would suspend or reduce enrichment: “No. We are not at that stage at all.” Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said it made no difference whether Washington wanted talks or war. Trump, having taken Vance off the file, is letting the blockade work: “At the request of the nations that I am looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a bit more civilly.”
global.geopolitical: Tehran has switched targets from shipping to the Gulf monarchies, and they have answered with a joint command and a compensation claim rather than mediation — closing the channel Qatar has carried since October.
global.socioeconomic: The squeeze lands on Iranians first: a vice-president conceded fuel stations cannot cover demand and drivers in Bandar Abbas blocked traffic over shortages. Gulf exports excluding Oman reached 18.4m barrels a day in October, 26 per cent below pre-war; Iran has exported almost no crude for two months.

global.headline: YEMEN'S GOVERNMENT GIVES UP THE SECOND CHOKEPOINT, AND THE HOUTHIS TAKE IT
summary: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces announced on Sunday they were pulling out of Dhubab airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area west of Taiz governorate, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis holding the ground above the strait between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The Southern Armed Forces called it a redeployment to secure Aden and strengthen other front lines. A Saudi-backed push last month had retaken Dhubab but never cleared the area or recovered al-Mocha, and Houthi gains around Taiz have reversed it. Saudi Arabia struck Houthi targets; the Houthis made no immediate comment. The movement has already shown it can close the waterway, and its missiles are fired at Saudi Arabia almost daily — one damaged an Aramco administrative building in Riyadh's financial district a week ago.
global.geopolitical: One aligned bloc now holds ground at both ends of the Suez-to-Asia route, the outcome nine months of naval deployments were meant to prevent, and a Hormuz settlement reached with Tehran would not bind the Houthis.
global.socioeconomic: Shipping that re-routed from the Red Sea to the Cape of Good Hope after 2023 had only partly returned; this makes the diversion the planning assumption again, adding roughly ten days and the fuel for them to every Asia-Europe voyage, and delivering later and dearer into Singapore and the Malacca ports at the far end of the lane.

global.headline: THE CHIP SCANDAL MOVES FROM NVIDIA TO THE COMMERCE DEPARTMENT, AND TO LUTNICK'S FAMILY FIRM
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that whether Nvidia had “a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions” matters more than Jensen Huang's affair, and asked whether it used shell companies to sell its most powerful chips to China: “These shell companies were obvious. They were being investigated.” He wants answers from Nvidia and its internal inquiry within ten days, and repeated that Treasury, State, the Pentagon and the US Trade Representative all favoured blacklisting Megaspeed while “Commerce had the pen”. A Justice Department criminal investigation is running, and Representative John Moolenaar said Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify before three House committees in one session, date unset.

The New York Times reported that Howard Lutnick pushed a narrower version of the rules on chips in overseas data centres — a higher computing-power threshold, future shipments only — and that one affected operator, Bitdeer, whose Malaysian A201 site opens in 2027 with hundreds of millions of dollars of Nvidia servers, is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm Lutnick handed to his sons. The paper found no evidence Cantor's interests shaped his decisions; Commerce says he divested entirely. Senator Chris Van Hollen said Lutnick “should be fired”. Megaspeed said Alice Huang left on 30 August 2025, denied wrongdoing and hired outside counsel; the Financial Times reported Huang has discussed returning as chief executive.
global.geopolitical: The question is no longer whether one executive was compromised but whether the department that writes American export controls can be trusted to write them — with Trump due in Shenzhen this week and Lutnick still expected on the trip.
global.socioeconomic: A Democratic Congress is seated in January with subpoena power over the licensing file, so what now deters a data-centre operator from buying American accelerators is not the entity list but the prospect of a retrospective inquiry — a cost-of-capital question for every Southeast Asian host, Singapore included.

global.headline: ESTONIA WILL SEAL ITS RUSSIAN BORDER AFTER AN ARSON ATTEMPT ON A DEFENCE FIRM
summary: Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December, Prime Minister Kristen Michal said on Sunday, after eight people were detained over an attempted arson attack on a defence-technology company overnight on Saturday. Nobody was hurt. Estonian security services say Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, ordered it. Russian intelligence “exploit border crossings to exert influence over people”, Michal said, and closing the border would “send a clear message that attacks on Estonia's defence industry and defence capabilities are unacceptable”. He did not say when they would reopen. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the attempt showed “Russia's hostile activities extend far beyond Ukraine” and that he expected further sanctions on Russian individuals and entities at Monday's EU foreign ministers' meeting in Brussels. Moscow's spokeswoman Maria Zakharova called the move “aggressive and unbridled Russophobia”; Ukraine's Andrii Sybiha said Estonia had shown that Russian sabotage “can and should have consequences beyond diplomatic condemnation”.
global.geopolitical: It is the first time a NATO state has answered the hybrid campaign by closing a national border rather than expelling diplomats, setting a template the Baltic and Nordic states can copy without an alliance decision — while American envoys offer Moscow a security architecture premised on the opposite trajectory.
global.socioeconomic: Narva and Koidula carry local traffic, dual nationals and families rather than much freight, so the cost falls on border towns and on the roughly quarter of Estonia's population that is Russian-speaking.

global.headline: ISRAEL KILLS A THIRD RAFAH BRIGADE COMMANDER AS FOUR ALLIES DEMAND GAZA'S TENTS BE LET IN
summary: Israel killed Samir Mahmoud Abu Younis, commander of Hamas's Rafah Brigade, in southern Gaza overnight on Saturday. He had replaced Nael Abu Obeid, killed in September, who had replaced Mohammad Sabaneh, killed in May 2025. Al-Qassam Brigades said Abu Younis joined in 1991 and helped plan the 7 October 2023 attack. Defence Minister Israel Katz said the policy continues “until Gaza is demilitarised and there is no Hamas”. The Palestinian health ministry counts more than 1,600 killed in near-daily strikes since the ceasefire was signed a year ago; days earlier a strike on Nasser Hospital's surgery unit killed six, including a doctor and a 13-year-old boy awaiting surgery, and injured 40.

In a joint statement on Sunday the foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom said 150,000 tents and other vital supplies were being held at the border, demanding “immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access” and entry for dual-use items. Israel says more than 91,000 tents went in ahead of winter but still bars the heavy equipment needed to clear rubble: “The reconstruction of Gaza can only begin after Hamas fully disarms.” Seasonal rains swamped tens of thousands of tents last week. The Board of Peace remains sidelined, its Palestinian technocratic committee not yet in the enclave and its security force unformed.
global.geopolitical: Decapitation has been run three times on one brigade in eighteen months and produced a replacement each time; what is new is that four of Israel's own partners have put their names to a public demand, moving the aid question from UN agencies to allied capitals.
global.socioeconomic: Nearly two million people are displaced into a winter with 150,000 tents stopped at a crossing, and without excavators there is no clearance, so no reconstruction labour market and no return.

global.headline: A VULCAN ROCKET FAILS AND TAKES FORTY OF AMAZON'S SATELLITES WITH IT
summary: A Vulcan rocket belonging to United Launch Alliance, the Boeing-Lockheed Martin joint venture, failed about ten minutes after lifting off from Space Launch Complex 41 in Florida on Sunday, destroying 40 satellites for Amazon's Leo internet constellation. The vehicle “suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit”, ULA said, adding that it had no data yet on the cause. It is the first outright mission failure in the company's twenty-year history, and Vulcan's first flight in nine months. Amazon said ULA “has been a trusted partner… and we believe they'll learn from this mission”. The loss comes a day after SpaceX caught a returning Starship upper stage with its launch tower.
global.geopolitical: Washington spent a decade trying not to depend on a single launch provider for national-security payloads, and Vulcan was the answer; a grounding of unknown length puts Space Force missions back in a queue behind commercial Falcon flights.
global.socioeconomic: Amazon's constellation was already behind the regulatory schedule requiring most of it in orbit, and must now re-manufacture 40 satellites and re-book a ride — more months in which Starlink alone sets the price of satellite broadband.

singapore.headline: PM WONG ASKS ASEAN FOR A HAZE REGISTER AND A FASTER FUEL PACT BEFORE SINGAPORE TAKES THE CHAIR
summary: At the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila on 15 November, PM Lawrence Wong called for a regional platform to coordinate and share information on the companies behind fires that cause transboundary haze, saying the Singapore-Indonesia joint task force already does this and can be widened. “If anyone is caught doing this across ASEAN, we will share information, we will take action, and we will hold companies responsible.” He credited President Prabowo Subianto with unprecedented efforts, attributed this year's severity to climate change and an unusual El Nino, and noted Parliament's recent tightening of the haze law.

In the plenary he named three priorities. Digital integration: build on the Digital Economy Framework Agreement signed on 14 November, projected to double the regional digital economy to US$2 trillion (S$2.6 trillion) by 2030, and widen bilateral payment links such as Singapore-Malaysia into a regional network. Energy security: ratify the ASEAN Petroleum Security Agreement swiftly and prioritise the ASEAN Power Grid. And broader external partnerships. He recalled that May's Cebu summit almost did not happen because of the Hormuz closure and said the situation “continues to be highly volatile”. On the Thailand-Cambodia border he urged restraint and pledged support as Singapore takes over the ASEAN Observer Team; on Myanmar he said the bloc should offer a clearer roadmap while Naypyidaw shows readiness to work with it.
singapore.geopolitical: Singapore is converting a bilateral enforcement mechanism into a regional one before it holds the gavel, and in taking the Observer Team and the Myanmar file it inherits the two disputes that have most damaged ASEAN consensus.
singapore.socioeconomic: The 2026 haze cost Singapore S$2.32 billion to 31 October, 4 per cent above 2015, so a register of culpable companies is a fiscal instrument as much as a diplomatic one — and the petroleum pact is the same argument in another commodity, a claim on neighbours' fuel made before the next closure rather than during it.

singapore.headline: MONUMENT CHURCHES AND TEMPLES GET SIXTY-YEAR LEASES, DOUBLE THE USUAL TENURE
summary: A policy change lets places of worship gazetted as national monuments renew their leases for up to 60 years, against the up-to-30 the Government generally grants places of worship on state land, the Singapore Land Authority and National Heritage Board confirmed. St Joseph's Church in Victoria Street, whose 99-year lease was to expire in February 2028, took a 60-year renewal from 15 July at a premium of more than S$5 million — paid soon after a five-year restoration costing about S$25 million that reopened in 2022. St George's Church in Minden Road and Tan Si Chong Su, the ancestral hall and temple in Magazine Road, have also been offered 60 years.

The agencies said monument owners face higher costs because preservation rules require compatible materials, traditional techniques and specialist craftsmen — St Joseph's hired a Portuguese restorer for artefacts no Singapore specialist could treat — and that longer tenure gives “greater certainty for long-term investments” while “balancing the need to retain planning flexibility”. Renewals stay case-by-case, priced on location, land and floor area, allowable use and tenure. Of Singapore's 77 national monuments, 30 are places of worship: 13 freehold, 11 on 999-year leases, one to 2092, and five on shorter terms, including Hajjah Fatimah Mosque and Prinsep Street Presbyterian Church, which renewed for 30 years in October 2023.
singapore.geopolitical: Heritage policy here is also religious-harmony policy: the five monuments on short leases are Catholic, Anglican, Chinese and Muslim, and a tenure rule applied unevenly would be read communally — 60 years for the whole class removes that reading without conceding freehold.
singapore.socioeconomic: Congregations fund restoration and premium alike from donations, so a renewal landing on the heels of a S$25 million restoration is a second capital call on the same parishioners; 60 years lets a monument amortise conservation across a generation.

word.definition: A sea or waterway treated as closed — under the exclusive control of one state, which may bar others from passage. Its opposite is mare liberum, the free sea open to all.
word.etymology: Latin, “closed sea”, from John Selden's treatise Mare Clausum of 1635, written for England's claim to the surrounding seas in answer to Hugo Grotius's Mare Liberum of 1609, which held that no nation can own the ocean. The quarrel between those titles is the origin of the modern law of the sea.
word.example: With Iranian drones over Bahrain and Yemeni government forces abandoning the heights above Bab el-Mandeb, both ends of the Suez route look less like free passage than mare clausum, held by whoever is willing to shoot.
